newsitem.title: UK: Sizzling tanker rates hike the cost of oil in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Sizzling tanker rates hike the cost of oil in Asia.

text.p: Chartering rates for Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) sailing from the Middle East to Asia are sky-high and should remain so until mid-August but the subsequent price fall should not be as sharp as last year, analysts and shipbrokers said.
A 250,000 tonne VLCC, the Ocean Guardian, was chartered this week to carry oil from the Mideast to Japan at a Worldscale rate of around 85, over $10 per tonne.
That compares with Worldscale rates of just 47 in April, or $5.50 a tonne, according to Reuters data calculated from a basket of shipbrokers' daily quotes.

"You would expect a pick-up at this time of year," said analyst Mark Jenkins at shipbrokers Simpson, Spence and Young, citing the winding down of summer refinery maintenance schedules in Asia which was boosting demand for crude oil.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) Japanese refinery maintenance programmes ran at around 1.25 million barrels per day (bpd) of primary distillation capacity in June. This would have fallen to less than half a million in July, and then just 200,000 bpd in August, the IEA estimated.
"You can see that in two months more than a million bpd of capacity will have returned (just from Japan,)" Jenkins said.
He added that Asian refiners were also anticipating a rise in oil demand as winter returns to the northern hemisphere later this year, and they were now importing oil to build their inventories.
"The effect is most spectacularly obvious for VLCCs than anywhere else but given a bit of time we will see some kind of domino effect into other types of tankers."

Brokers Galbraith's Ltd said in a weekly report that rates for VLCCs were likely to fall off in August, noting that last year the "hot market" ended in the second week of August and Worldscale rates for VLCCs fell back into the low 50s by the end of September.

Jenkins said that VLCC Worldscale rates reached the mid-70s last year but another, longer term factor was also at work which had booted this year's rates further and meant rates were unlikely to fall as far as last year.
"There is a greater fussiness now on the part of the charterers, particularly the South Koreans," he said.

A series of coastal oil spills in coastal South Korean waters in the last two and a half years, he said, had led to a tightening of the quality requirements for ships and this had boosted rates as older, cheaper ships were increasingly prohibited from Asian ports.

Shipbuilders have responded to the new demand, he said, but added that the anticipated surge in new tankers is yet to arrive. "There has been a dramatic turnaround in the ordering of new tankers to the point where the industry may be in another unsubstantiated building boom. This is the case for all sizes of tankers."

"But at the moment the actual volumes of new-building tonnage which is being delivered is lower than for some time," he said, adding that the surge of current orders would not be seen at the ends of the production lines before late 1998 or 1999.
"I think rates for VLCCs will fall to some extent by the middle of August but not necessarily to the degree where we could say the market is getting flabby."
